intervals.label: concept and community recommendation
intervals.note: The history page says planning began in the early 1990s and that a 2001 report recommended the telescope (then the Large-Aperture Synoptic Survey Telescope) as a major initiative; no formal proposal date is given.
intervals.quote: a 2001 report by the Astronomy and Astrophysics Survey Committee

intervals.label: construction
intervals.note: The page's photo caption dates the 'First Stone' event to April 2015; the text gives only the year. End is the October 2025 transition to operations.
intervals.quote: In 2015 a traditional stone-laying ceremony was held on Cerro Pachón, in Chile, to commemorate the official start of construction.

intervals.label: operations
intervals.locator: Rubin 'History' page, section 'From construction to operations'
intervals.quote: in October 2025, Rubin Observatory reached another defining moment: the official transition from construction to operations.

website.quote: NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, jointly funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, is a brand new astronomy and astrophysics facility on Cerro Pachón in Chile.

name: Vera C. Rubin Observatory
notes: The facility was named the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST) before December 2019; the Rubin history page dates the Congressional act confirming the new name to December 2019.

operator.quote: Rubin Observatory is operated by NSF NOIRLab and SLAC.
operator.value: NSF NOIRLab and SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory

altitude.locator: NOIRLab Simonyi Survey Telescope page, 'Location' table

summary.plain: A new observatory on Cerro Pachón in Chile, named for astronomer Vera Rubin. Its telescope and the largest digital camera ever built photograph the southern sky every few nights.
summary.technical: NSF–DOE observatory on Cerro Pachón, Chile, operated by NSF NOIRLab and SLAC; houses the 8.4-m Simonyi Survey Telescope and LSST Camera for the 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time.
